title: Utanga
body:
Utanga

Having completed the instruction of the grandsire, Sree Krishna bade farewell to the Pandavas and set off in His chariot toward Dwaraka. As He coursed across the sandy plains, He met His childhood friend, the simple and austere Brahmana Utanga. Coming down from His chariot, Krishna prostrated before the holy sage. After the customary greetings were exchanged, Utanga, unaware of the war's conclusion, asked about the welfare of their Kuru kinsmen.
When Krishna narrated the complete annihilation of the Kuru and Panchala dynasties, Utanga's chest heaved with righteous indignation. His eyes turned red with anger; he raised his hand to curse the Lord: 'Vasudeva, were you there standing by and did you let all this happen? You possess infinite power, yet you did not prevent this slaughter of brothers. You have surely practised deceit and led them to destruction. Prepare now to receive my curse!'
Krishna smiled with absolute serenity: 'Peace, peace! Calm yourself. Do not use up the fruit of your great penances in this anger. Listen to my words, and then, if you still like, you may pronounce your curse.' The Lord then revealed His Visvarupa—the cosmic form encompassing all creation, time, and space. He explained that everything that takes place in Prakriti moves according to the irreversible laws of nature and individual karma, which are but manifestations of His supreme will. Utanga, overwhelmed by this vision, bowed in humble submission and requested forgiveness.
Delighted by Utanga's realisation, Krishna offered him a boon. The simple, desert-dwelling Brahmana replied, 'Well, my Lord, if you must give me some boon, let me find water to drink whenever I might feel thirsty in this dry desert. Give me this boon.' Sree Krishna smiled, granted the boon, and went on His way.
Days later, feeling parched in the desert, Utanga remembered the boon. Suddenly, a dirty, half-naked outcaste (Chandala) appeared, surrounded by howling dogs, carrying a wet leather bag containing muddy, unclean water. The Chandala offered the water to the proud Brahmana. Utanga, blinded by his ritual prejudices and intellectual pride, rejected the outcaste's water with disgust.
The Chandala vanished, and Sree Krishna appeared in his place with conch and discus. Utanga cried out in bitter disappointment: 'O Purushottama, you put me to a difficult trial! Was it right of you to make an untouchable offer unclean water to me, a Brahmana?'
Krishna smiled sadly: 'O Utanga, for your sake, I asked Lord Indra to take the nectar of immortality (Amrita) to you in the guise of water. Indra refused, saying that Amrita cannot be given to a mortal. But I prevailed upon him. Indra agreed on one condition—that he would present it as an outcaste to test your spiritual understanding. I accepted the challenge, believing you had attained true knowledge (Jnana) and transcended external, physical illusions. But you failed the test, rejecting the nectar of immortality because of your superficial prejudices.' Utanga, weeping in shame, fell at the Lord's feet, realising that true wisdom must perceive the Divine equally in all beings.
